title: Carboxylic Acids and Their Derivatives
description: Acidity, nucleophilic acyl substitution, esters, amides, anhydrides, acyl chlorides and nitriles.
overview: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives are the oxidation level that lies a step above aldehydes and ketones. They include fats and oils (esters), proteins (amides), aspirin, nylon and polyester, and they are the point where most synthetic routes finish. All of them undergo one reaction type, nucleophilic acyl substitution, in which a nucleophile replaces the group attached to the carbonyl.

This chapter covers the acidity and preparation of carboxylic acids, the mechanism of nucleophilic acyl substitution and the reactivity order of the derivatives, the interconversions among them, and their reductions, with an eye on biological examples such as the peptide bond and soap.
objectives: Name carboxylic acids and derivatives, and explain the acidity of RCOOH.
Write the addition–elimination mechanism of nucleophilic acyl substitution and rank derivatives by reactivity.
Interconvert acids, acyl chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides.
Distinguish acid-catalyzed and base-promoted ester hydrolysis (saponification).
Reduce derivatives to alcohols, aldehydes, amines and ketones with the right reagents.
Describe the chemistry of nitriles, and the peptide bond.

sections.title: Carboxylic acids
body: A **carboxylic acid** (R–COOH) has a carbonyl and a hydroxyl on the same carbon. Names use -oic acid (ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, or acetic acid; benzoic acid for PhCOOH). The carbon is numbered C1. Carboxylic acids are extensively hydrogen bonded: they form dimers even in the gas phase, so their boiling points are higher than alcohols of comparable mass (propanoic acid 141 °C against propan-1-ol 97 °C), and acids up to four carbons are miscible with water.

They are far more acidic than alcohols (pK_a 4–5 against 16). The conjugate base, the **carboxylate**, is stabilized by resonance, which spreads the negative charge equally over two oxygens (both C–O bonds are 126 pm, between C–O and C=O lengths). Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity (chloroacetic acid pK_a 2.87, trifluoroacetic acid 0.5), and benzoic acid (4.2) is slightly stronger than acetic acid (4.76). A carboxylic acid is deprotonated by bicarbonate (pK_a of H₂CO₃ 6.4), so acids can be separated from neutral compounds by extraction into aqueous NaHCO₃.

list: Oxidation of a primary alcohol or aldehyde (Jones, KMnO₄).
Oxidative cleavage of alkenes and alkynes; side-chain oxidation of alkylbenzenes (KMnO₄).
Hydrolysis of nitriles, R–C≡N + H₃O⁺ → R–COOH, which also extends a chain by one carbon after SN2 with cyanide.
Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent: R–MgBr + CO₂, then H₃O⁺.

body: Long-chain acids occur in fats as **fatty acids** (palmitic C₁₆, stearic C₁₈, oleic C₁₈ with one cis C=C). Acids α-halogenate in the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction (Br₂, PBr₃), giving α-bromo acids that can be converted to α-amino acids by SN2 with ammonia.

check.a: The acetate ion has its charge delocalized over two oxygens
wrong: Acetic acid has a stronger O–H bond

sections.title: Nucleophilic acyl substitution
terms: leaving group ability in acyl substitution
body: Acid derivatives have the form R–C(=O)–L, where L is a leaving group: Cl (acyl chloride), OC(=O)R (anhydride), OR′ (ester), NR′₂ (amide) and, in the acid itself, OH. Nucleophiles attack the carbonyl carbon as in aldehydes and ketones, but the tetrahedral intermediate, having a potential leaving group, can collapse by expelling it and regenerating C=O: an **addition–elimination** mechanism called **nucleophilic acyl substitution**. Aldehydes and ketones have only H or R, which are not leaving groups, so they undergo addition instead.

The reaction goes forward when the new group is a poorer leaving group than the one it replaces. The result is a reactivity order that parallels leaving-group ability, which is the reverse of basicity, and also depends on how much the lone pair on L stabilizes the carbonyl by resonance (strong for nitrogen, weak for chlorine):

head: Derivative
Leaving group
Conjugate acid pK_a
Relative reactivity
table.caption: A more reactive derivative can be converted into any less reactive one, but not the reverse without activation.

body.key: A more reactive derivative can be converted to a less reactive one directly. Acyl chlorides give anhydrides, esters and amides, and esters give amides, but amides do not give esters without forcing conditions.

check.q: Which derivative is most reactive toward nucleophiles?
Why do aldehydes and ketones undergo addition rather than substitution?
check.a: They have no good leaving group on the carbonyl carbon

sections.title: Interconversion of the derivatives
body: Thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) or oxalyl chloride converts a carboxylic acid to an **acyl chloride**, with SO₂ and HCl as gas by-products. Acyl chlorides are the usual starting point for making other derivatives, because they react readily with water (to the acid), alcohols (esters), amines (amides) and carboxylates (anhydrides). Use pyridine or excess amine to take up the HCl.

The **Fischer esterification** heats a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and a strong acid catalyst: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O. All steps are reversible, with K about 4 for acetic acid and ethanol, so the equilibrium is driven by using excess alcohol or removing water. The mechanism is acid activation of the carbonyl, addition of the alcohol, proton transfer, and loss of water. Esters are also made from acyl chlorides or anhydrides with an alcohol, and by SN2 of a carboxylate on a primary halide. Aspirin is made by **acetylation** of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride. Intramolecular esters are **lactones** and intramolecular amides are **lactams** (penicillin has a β-lactam).

**Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis** is the reverse of Fischer esterification, driven by excess water, and is reversible. **Base-promoted hydrolysis (saponification)** uses hydroxide: HO⁻ adds to the carbonyl, the tetrahedral intermediate expels alkoxide, and the resulting acid is immediately deprotonated by the alkoxide or hydroxide to the carboxylate. That last step is irreversible, so saponification goes to completion. Hydrolysis of a fat (a triester of glycerol and fatty acids) with NaOH gives glycerol and soap, the sodium salts of the fatty acids. One full equivalent of base is consumed.

Amides are made from acyl chlorides or anhydrides and amines (two equivalents of amine, or one plus a tertiary amine). A carboxylic acid and an amine give only an ammonium carboxylate salt at room temperature, so direct amide formation needs heat or an activating agent. **Coupling reagents** such as **DCC** (dicyclohexylcarbodiimide) activate the acid as an O-acylisourea, and this is how peptide bonds are made in the laboratory. Amides are the least reactive derivatives: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl (the C–N bond is partial double, with a rotation barrier of about 75 kJ mol⁻¹), so the amide is planar, neutral (not basic) and resistant to hydrolysis. Boiling in strong acid or base for hours is required. This stability is why the **peptide bond** of proteins is robust, and also why proteins are hydrolyzed by enzymes (proteases) under mild conditions.

example.title: Choosing a route to an ester
example.problem: Prepare methyl benzoate by two routes.
example.solution: (1) Fischer: benzoic acid, excess methanol, catalytic H₂SO₄, reflux, with excess alcohol to drive the equilibrium. (2) Acyl chloride: benzoic acid with SOCl₂ to give benzoyl chloride, then methanol with pyridine; this is irreversible and works at room temperature.

check.a: The carboxylic acid product is deprotonated to the unreactive carboxylate
wrong: The alcohol is removed by distillation

check.q: Why are amides so resistant to hydrolysis?
check.a: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, and the amide anion is a poor leaving group

check.q: A fat treated with NaOH gives…
check.a: Glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids (soap)

sections.title: Reduction of acid derivatives, and nitriles
terms: lithium aluminum hydride reduction of esters
body: Acid derivatives are reduced by hydrides, though their oxidation level lies above aldehydes. The product depends on the reagent and the derivative.

head: Derivative
LiAlH₄
DIBAL-H, −78 °C
R′MgX or R′Li
table.caption: Products of reducing and organometallic additions to acid derivatives.

body: Esters and acyl chlorides react twice with a Grignard reagent, because the intermediate ketone is more reactive than the starting ester. A **Weinreb amide** (RCON(OMe)Me) stops at the ketone, since its tetrahedral intermediate is stabilized by chelation of the magnesium and does not collapse until workup. **DIBAL-H** (diisobutylaluminum hydride), at −78 °C and one equivalent, reduces an ester to an aldehyde and stops, since the tetrahedral aluminum intermediate persists until hydrolysis.

**Nitriles** (R–C≡N) have an sp carbon and a strong dipole. They are made by SN2 of cyanide on a primary or secondary halide, by dehydration of a primary amide (SOCl₂ or P₂O₅), and from aryl diazonium salts (Sandmeyer). They behave as carboxylic acid derivatives: **hydrolysis** with aqueous acid or base, through an amide, gives a carboxylic acid; LiAlH₄ reduces them to primary amines, and Grignard reagents add once to give ketones after hydrolysis of the imine. Nitriles are the standard way to add one carbon.

example.title: Chain extension
example.problem: Convert 1-bromobutane into pentanoic acid and into pentan-1-amine.
example.solution: Treat 1-bromobutane with NaCN in DMSO (SN2) to give pentanenitrile. Hydrolysis with aqueous acid and heat gives pentanoic acid, and reduction with LiAlH₄ gives pentan-1-amine (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂).

check.q: Which reagent stops at the aldehyde stage when reducing an ester?

quiz.q: Chloroacetic acid has pK_a 2.87 and acetic acid has pK_a 4.76. About how many times larger is the K_a of chloroacetic acid?
quiz.why: The ratio of K_a values is 10^(4.76 − 2.87) = 10^1.89 ≈ 78. The electron-withdrawing chlorine stabilizes the carboxylate; reading the pK_a difference as a ratio gives the common error of about 2.

quiz.q: In sodium acetate, what are the two C–O bonds of the carboxylate group like?
quiz.a: Identical, each between a single and a double bond in length (about 126 pm)
wrong: One short C=O and one long C–O⁻, since the charge sits on one oxygen
Both as short as the C=O bond of a ketone, since the carbon is sp²
Both as long as the C–O bond of an alcohol, since the anion has no double bond
quiz.why: The negative charge is delocalized equally over the two oxygens by resonance, so the two bonds cannot differ. This delocalization is the reason carboxylic acids are so much more acidic than alcohols.

quiz.q: An ether solution of phenol (pK_a 10) and benzoic acid (pK_a 4.2) is shaken with aqueous NaHCO₃ (conjugate acid H₂CO₃, pK_a 6.4). What passes into the aqueous layer?
wrong: Both sodium benzoate and sodium phenoxide
Neither, since bicarbonate is too weak a base to deprotonate any acid
quiz.why: Bicarbonate removes a proton only from an acid with a pK_a below about 6.4. Benzoic acid qualifies, whereas phenol stays in the ether.

quiz.q: Which sequence converts bromobenzene into benzoic acid?
quiz.a: Mg in ether, then CO₂, then H₃O⁺
wrong: NaCN in DMSO, then H₃O⁺ and heat
quiz.why: The aryl bromide forms a Grignard reagent, which carboxylates with CO₂. NaCN does not displace halide from an unactivated aryl ring by SN2, and KMnO₄ needs a benzylic C–H.

quiz.q: An acyl chloride reacts with water much faster than an amide does. The best explanation is that
quiz.a: Cl⁻ is a very weak base and a good leaving group, and Cl donates little to the carbonyl
wrong: the amide carbonyl carbon is sp³ hybridized, which hinders attack by the water nucleophile
the C–Cl bond is much weaker than the C–N bond, and bond energy alone sets the rate
water cannot hydrogen-bond to the carbonyl oxygen of an amide, so it is never activated
quiz.why: In addition–elimination the tetrahedral intermediate must expel L. Chloride is an excellent leaving group and offers weak resonance stabilization, whereas the amide nitrogen donates strongly and R₂N⁻ is a terrible leaving group.

quiz.q: Which conversion proceeds readily under mild conditions without special activation?
quiz.why: A more reactive derivative converts to a less reactive one. Each wrong option runs uphill from amide to anhydride or ester, or from ester to acyl chloride.

quiz.q: Why is SOCl₂ convenient for converting a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride?
quiz.a: The by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases that leave the mixture
wrong: The by-product is water, which is easily separated by extraction
SOCl₂ acts as a catalyst and is recovered unchanged at the end
The only by-product is NaCl, which precipitates and is filtered off
quiz.why: RCOOH + SOCl₂ → RCOCl + SO₂ + HCl. Both by-products escape as gases, which also drives the reaction to completion.

quiz.q: Equimolar acid and alcohol are heated with an acid catalyst. For this esterification K = 9. What fraction of the acid is converted to ester at equilibrium?
quiz.why: With conversion x, K = x²/(1 − x)² = 9, so x/(1 − x) = 3 and x = 0.75. Using K = 4 would give 67%, and 25% is the fraction that remains.

quiz.q: How many moles of NaOH are needed to saponify 0.20 mol of a fat (a triester of glycerol) completely?
quiz.why: Each ester group consumes one hydroxide, because the acid product is deprotonated to the carboxylate. The fat has three ester groups, so 3 × 0.20 = 0.60 mol.

quiz.q: Why do carboxylate ions resist nucleophilic acyl substitution?
quiz.a: The negative charge repels an incoming nucleophile, and O²⁻ would have to leave
wrong: The carboxylate carbon is not electrophilic, since it is sp³ hybridized after resonance
Carboxylates are too basic to be attacked by any nucleophile at all, even a strong one
The two oxygens form a stable chelate with any metal ion present in the mixture
quiz.why: Attack on a negatively charged group is disfavored electrostatically, and O²⁻ is an extremely poor leaving group. That makes carboxylates the least reactive acyl species.

quiz.q: Propanoic acid is mixed with ethylamine at 25 °C. The main product is
quiz.why: Proton transfer from the acid to the amine is instantaneous. The carboxylate is unreactive toward the ammonium ion, so an amide needs heat or an activating agent.

quiz.q: Which statement about the amide group is correct?
quiz.a: The C–N bond has partial double-bond character, so C, N and their substituents are coplanar
wrong: The nitrogen is pyramidal, and rotation about the C–N bond is as easy as in an amine
Amides are more basic than amines, since the carbonyl oxygen donates to nitrogen
The nitrogen lone pair is fully available, which makes amides good N-nucleophiles
quiz.why: Delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair into C=O (rotation barrier about 75 kJ mol⁻¹) makes the unit planar and removes the basicity and nucleophilicity of the nitrogen.

quiz.q: DCC is added to a mixture of a carboxylic acid and an amine. Its role is to
quiz.a: convert the OH of the acid into a good leaving group (an O-acylisourea)
wrong: protonate the amine so that it becomes a stronger nucleophile toward the acid
remove the water that forms, by distillation from the reaction mixture
reduce the acid to the aldehyde before the amine is added to the flask
quiz.why: Activating the acid avoids the unreactive carboxylate salt and lets the amine attack the carbonyl at room temperature. This is how peptide bonds are formed in the laboratory.

quiz.q: Methyl pentanoate is treated with excess PhMgBr, followed by H₃O⁺. The product is
wrong: 1-phenylpentan-1-one, from a single addition of the Grignard reagent
pentan-1-ol, from reduction of the ester by the Grignard reagent
quiz.why: The ester adds one PhMgBr, loses methoxide to give a ketone, and that ketone is more reactive than the ester and takes up a second Ph. The result is a tertiary alcohol with two identical groups from the Grignard reagent.

quiz.q: A Weinreb amide, RCON(OMe)Me, reacts with R′MgX to give a ketone and not a tertiary alcohol. Why?
quiz.a: Mg chelates the tetrahedral intermediate, which persists until workup, so no ketone is there to react again
wrong: The Grignard reagent cannot attack an amide carbonyl, so it just deprotonates the N–CH₃ group
The ketone product is deactivated toward further addition by the neighboring amide group
The methoxy group transfers hydride to the ketone as it forms and so destroys it
quiz.why: The stable chelated intermediate collapses only after aqueous workup. By then the Grignard reagent has been quenched, so a second addition cannot occur.

quiz.q: A primary amide RCONH₂ is heated with SOCl₂ or P₂O₅. The product is
wrong: the acyl chloride, RCOCl, with NH₃ lost
quiz.why: These reagents dehydrate a primary amide, removing the elements of water to give a nitrile. LiAlH₄ would be needed to reach the amine.

quiz.q: Which halide is unsuitable for making a nitrile by displacement with NaCN?
wrong: Benzyl bromide, a primary benzylic halide
quiz.why: Cyanide displaces halide by SN2, which works on primary and secondary carbons. A tertiary halide gives mainly elimination because cyanide is also basic.

quiz.q: Benzonitrile is treated with CH₃MgBr, and then H₃O⁺ is added. The product is
quiz.why: The Grignard reagent adds once to C≡N to give an imine salt, which is hydrolyzed on workup to the ketone. It does not add twice, as it would to an ester.

summary: Carboxylic acids (pK_a 4–5) are acidic because the carboxylate is resonance stabilized. They are made by oxidation, nitrile hydrolysis or Grignard carboxylation.
Acid derivatives undergo addition–elimination (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Reactivity: acyl chloride > anhydride > thioester > ester ≈ acid > amide > carboxylate.
SOCl₂ makes acyl chlorides. Fischer esterification is reversible and saponification is irreversible. Amides need an acyl chloride, heat or a coupling agent such as DCC.
LiAlH₄ reduces derivatives to alcohols (amides to amines). DIBAL-H and Weinreb amides stop at aldehyde or ketone. Esters add two equivalents of Grignard.
Nitriles add one carbon via SN2 with cyanide, and can be hydrolyzed to acids or reduced to amines.

problems.q: Predict the products: (a) benzoyl chloride + NH₃ (excess); (b) ethyl acetate + NaOH, H₂O, heat, then H₃O⁺; (c) ethyl benzoate + 2 CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺; (d) butanamide + LiAlH₄.
problems.solution: (a) Benzamide plus NH₄Cl. (b) Ethanol and acetic acid (acetate first, acid after workup). (c) 2-Phenylpropan-2-ol. (d) Butylamine (butan-1-amine).
problems.a: (a) benzamide; (b) ethanol and acetic acid; (c) 2-phenylpropan-2-ol; (d) butan-1-amine.

problems.q: Show how to prepare propanoic acid by two methods from 1-bromoethane.
problems.solution: (1) NaCN, DMSO gives propanenitrile; hydrolyze with aqueous acid and heat. (2) Mg, ether gives CH₃CH₂MgBr; CO₂, then H₃O⁺.
problems.a: Via the nitrile, or via the Grignard reagent and CO₂.

problems.q: Rank by increasing rate of hydrolysis: methyl acetate, acetyl chloride, acetamide, acetic anhydride.
problems.solution: Acetamide is slowest, then methyl acetate, then acetic anhydride, with acetyl chloride the fastest.
problems.a: Acetamide < methyl acetate < acetic anhydride < acetyl chloride.

problems.q: Explain why an ester made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol in a Fischer esterification has a yield limited to about 67% when using equimolar reagents (K = 4).
problems.solution: At equilibrium K = x²/(1 − x)² = 4, so x/(1 − x) = 2 and x = 0.67. Using a large excess of alcohol (10 equivalents) or removing water pushes the yield above 95%.
problems.a: The equilibrium constant of 4 limits the conversion to 67%.
